config.title: Build undo and redo for text editor state

intro.title: Build undo and redo for text editor state
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple text editor that supports undo and redo functionality, allowing users to revert or reapply changes to the text. You will learn how to manage application state using arrays to store a history of text snapshots. The core programming concept involves tracking the current state index and updating it with array methods like push and slice. You will use fundamental JavaScript constructs such as variables, event handlers, and DOM manipulation to create this interactive feature.
intro.usecase: The undo/redo pattern is essential in any application where users edit content and need to correct mistakes. You'll find this functionality in text editors like Google Docs and Notion, graphic design tools like Figma and Photoshop, and code editors like VS Code. As a developer, implementing undo/redo ensures users can confidently make changes without fear of permanent errors. This pattern also appears in form-heavy applications, spreadsheet tools, and any interface where data manipulation occurs frequently.

objectives: Initialize state variables to track current text, undo history, and redo history
Implement a function to update text state while preserving previous versions for undo
Construct an undo handler that restores previous text states and manages redo history
Build a redo handler that reapplies undone changes and updates history appropriately
Configure event handlers to trigger state updates on text input changes
Render UI controls that display undo/redo availability based on history state
Integrate undo and redo functionality into a complete text editor interface

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and useState from the 'react' library.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added at the top of the file, enabling the use of React and the useState hook.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' library.

steps.title: Create the main TextEditor component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TextEditor that returns an empty fragment for now.
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named TextEditor that returns an empty fragment: <> </> or <React.Fragment> </React.Fragment>.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create the TextEditor component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A TextEditor component is defined and returns an empty fragment.
successCriteria: The TextEditor component is created and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main TextEditor component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but make sure it's named exactly 'TextEditor' and returns an empty fragment.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Create a functional component named TextEditor that returns an empty fragment.

steps.title: Initialize the current text state
steps.instruction: Inside the TextEditor component, use useState to create a state variable named 'text' initialized to an empty string.
steps.hint: Call useState with an empty string as the initial value and destructure the returned array into 'text' and 'setText'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a state variable for user input
const [input, setInput] = useState('');
steps.expectedOutcome: The TextEditor component will have a state variable 'text' that starts as an empty string, ready to store the editor's current content.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with an empty string, and the returned array is destructured into 'text' and 'setText'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with an empty string and destructuring into 'text' and 'setText'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the TextEditor component, use useState to create a state variable named 'text' initialized to an empty string.

steps.title: Initialize the redo stack state
steps.instruction: Inside your TextEditor component, use useState to create a state variable named 'redoStack' and initialize it to an empty array.
steps.hint: Add another useState call similar to how you created the undoStack state, but name this one 'redoStack'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: another array state variable
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have three state variables: text, undoStack, and redoStack, all properly initialized.
successCriteria: A state variable named 'redoStack' is declared with useState and initialized to an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState to create a state variable named 'redoStack' and initializing it to an empty array.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a useState call inside the component to create a state variable named 'redoStack' initialized to an empty array.

steps.title: Define the handleTextChange function
steps.instruction: Inside your TextEditor component, define a function named handleTextChange that takes an event parameter. The function should: 1) Save the current text value to the undoStack, 2) Update the text state with the new value from the event, and 3) Clear the redoStack.
steps.hint: Remember to use setUndoStack to add the current text to the undo stack before updating the text state with setText. Use event.target.value to get the new text value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleTextChange function that properly manages the undo stack and updates text when the user types.
successCriteria: The handleTextChange function is defined, saves current text to undoStack, updates text state with event.target.value, and clears redoStack.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Your function is defined but may be missing one or more required actions: saving to undoStack, updating text state, or clearing redoStack.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleTextChange function is not properly defined or missing. Review the requirements: save current text to undoStack, update text with event.target.value, and clear redoStack.

steps.title: Define the handleRedo function
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleRedo inside your TextEditor component. This function should check if there are items in the redoStack, and if so: move the current text to the undoStack, pop the last state from redoStack, and set it as the current text.
steps.hint: Follow the same pattern as handleUndo but work with the redoStack instead. Use setRedoStack and setUndoStack to update the stacks, and setText to update the current text.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleRedo function that can restore text from the redo stack when called.
successCriteria: The handleRedo function is defined, checks if redoStack has items, moves current text to undoStack, pops from redoStack, and sets the popped value as the new text.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined handleRedo, but it might be missing one of the required actions: checking the stack, moving text to undo, popping from redo, or setting the text.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleRedo function is not defined or doesn't follow the required logic. Review the steps: check redoStack, move current text to undoStack, pop from redoStack, set text.

steps.title: Add the textarea and wire its onChange
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your TextEditor component, add a textarea element. Set its value attribute to the text state and its onChange event handler to call handleTextChange.
steps.hint: The textarea should be a self-closing JSX element. Use value={text} and onChange={handleTextChange}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: textarea with value and onChange
<textarea value={inputText} onChange={handleInputChange} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now render a textarea that displays the current text and calls the change handler when edited.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a textarea element with value={text} and onChange={handleTextChange}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a textarea, but check that both value and onChange are correctly set.
steps.feedbackWrong: The textarea is missing or not properly connected. Make sure to include value={text} and onChange={handleTextChange}.

steps.title: Add undo and redo buttons and wire their onClick events
steps.instruction: Add two button elements below the textarea: one labeled 'Undo' and one labeled 'Redo'. Wire their onClick events to call handleUndo and handleRedo respectively.
steps.hint: Place the buttons after the textarea in the return statement. Use <button> elements with appropriate text and onClick handlers.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI now includes two buttons below the textarea: 'Undo' and 'Redo', each wired to their respective handler functions.
successCriteria: Two button elements are present with labels 'Undo' and 'Redo', and their onClick events are correctly wired to handleUndo and handleRedo.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added buttons, but check that both have correct labels and onClick handlers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons are missing or not correctly wired. Ensure you have two <button> elements with onClick={handleUndo} and onClick={handleRedo}.
